text: Lucas Valeriu Ntuba Radebe OIS (born 12 April 1969) is a South African former professional footballer who played as a centre back. Born to Emily and Johannes Radebe in the Diepkloof section of Soweto, near Johannesburg, he is one of 11 children and attended Bopasenatla Secondary School until age 15. His parents sent him to Bophuthatswana for Grade 10 to protect him from the violence in Diepkloof Zone Four, where he attended Ngotwane High School near Zeerust. He began playing in the now-defunct Bophuthatswana Soccer League (BOPSOL) with Stocks Birds in Lehurutshe, closer to Zeerust, before being scouted by Kaizer Chiefs in South Africa. Initially a goalkeeper, he switched to central midfield and then to central defence. In 1989, Patrick Ntsoelengoe recruited him to Kaizer Chiefs, where he became captain during his time at the club. In 1994, Radebe and Philemon "Chippa" Masinga moved to Leeds United for a transfer fee of £250,000; Radebe was included in the deal to please Masinga, though he became the more valuable player. Initially, the move was unsuccessful due to disagreements with then-Leeds manager Howard Wilkinson and injuries that prevented him from securing a regular first-team spot. In March 1996, he returned to goalkeeping after John Lukic's injury and again played in goal when Mark Beeney was sent off against Manchester United, earning 'cult-hero' status despite Leeds losing 1–0. When Wilkinson was replaced by George Graham, Radebe's career flourished, and he was made captain for the 1998–99 season. During that season, Leeds finished fourth in the FA Premier League and qualified for the UEFA Cup; in 1999–2000, they finished third and qualified for the Champions League, reaching the semi-finals. Radebe turned down offers to join Manchester United, AC Milan, and Roma. In 2000, he was awarded the FIFA Fair Play Award and also received the Contribution to the Community Award in the Premier League 10 Seasons Awards. That same year, he sustained serious knee and ankle injuries, missing nearly two years and struggling to regain form. He made his international debut for South Africa on 7 July 1992 against Cameroon and was part of the 1996 African Cup of Nations-winning squad. He captained South Africa at the 1998 and 2002 FIFA World Cups, though the team failed to reach the knockout stages in both; he scored a goal in 2002. He earned 70 caps and scored two goals, with his last match being against England on 22 May 2003. After retiring in May 2005, Leeds held a testimonial match at Elland Road on 2 May 2005, attended by over 37,886 fans, and he also played in a retirement match in Durban, with proceeds donated to charity. In August 2006, Radebe returned to Leeds after failing to secure a role in South Africa's 2010 World Cup preparations, stating he was "tired of waiting for unreliable people" who had promised him a position in the national team setup. In 2008, a Leeds brewery named a beer "Radebeer," reflecting fan admiration. On 8 October 2009, he was named an ambassador by the English Football Association to support the 2018 World Cup bid. A biography, *Lucas: From the Streets of Soweto to Soccer Superstar* by Richard Coomber, was published in 2010. In May 2010, he won the PFA Merit Award for his contributions to football. During the 2010 FIFA World Cup, he served as a pundit for ITV and a columnist for The Daily Telegraph. In September 2010, he expressed interest in managing Leeds United and the South African national team, stating those were the only coaching roles he would consider. In July 2012, he accepted a position as team manager with the South African national side. In October 2013, he was set to return to Elland Road, where he was presented to the crowd on 30 October 2013. On 23 January 2013, it was confirmed that boxer Josh Warrington would fight IBF world champion Lee Selby on 19 May at Elland Road, with Radebe joining Warrington for the ringwalk; Warrington won by split decision, and the band Kaiser Chiefs performed songs at the event. In 1991, while driving with his brother Lazarus to buy drinks for his mother, Radebe was shot; the bullet entered his back and exited halfway down his thigh, but he was not critically injured. The incident, which he attributes to someone being hired to prevent him from switching clubs, influenced his decision to join Leeds United in 1994. He was voted 54th in the Top 100 Great South Africans in 2004. His wife Feziwe died of cancer in October 2008; in December 2008, he was treated for a heart complaint after collapsing at the gym. He married his second wife at the end of 2015. The British indie/britpop band Kaiser Chiefs chose their name because Radebe is a former player of Kaizer Chiefs. Radebe has been an ambassador for FIFA's SOS Children's Villages and received the FIFA Fair Play Award in December 2000 for his efforts in eliminating racism in football and his work with children in South Africa.
